nameStory: Swamp cottonwood gets its name from its love of wet, soggy places where other cottonwoods can't survive - it's the swamp specialist of the poplar family! The 'cottonwood' part comes from the fluffy, cotton-like seeds that float through the air in late spring, creating what looks like a gentle snowstorm on warm days.
description: Swamp cottonwood is a large deciduous tree that can handle what other trees can't - standing water and soggy soil. This member of the willow family grows into a substantial tree with a broad, rounded crown. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special for nature enthusiasts. Like its poplar relatives, it's a fast-growing tree that provides important habitat for wildlife.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with a soft, downy feel on the undersides (hence 'downy poplar'). The leaf edges have small, rounded teeth, and they're arranged alternately on branches. When you flip a leaf over and run your finger across it, you'll feel distinctly fuzzy.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young bark is smooth and greenish-gray, becoming darker and developing shallow furrows with age. The bark often has a slightly bitter, medicinal smell when scratched - characteristic of the willow family.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a large tree with a broad, spreading crown. Branches tend to be somewhat droopy or pendulous, especially on older trees. Often grows in small clumps or groves rather than as isolated specimens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces drooping catkins in early spring before leaves emerge. Male and female flowers appear on separate trees, with male catkins being longer and more showy.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Releases masses of white, cotton-like seeds in late spring that float on the breeze. Seeds are attached to fluffy white hairs that help them travel long distances to find suitable wet spots.

habitat: Swamp cottonwood thrives in wetlands, swamps, and areas with standing or slow-moving water where other poplars struggle. Look for it along pond edges, in seasonal wetlands, and in areas that flood regularly. It's extremely rare in New England, with most sightings in southern portions of the region where it reaches the northern edge of its range.

seasonality.spring: Drooping catkins appear in early spring before the leaves, followed by the emergence of heart-shaped leaves with their characteristic fuzzy undersides. Late spring brings clouds of cotton-like seeds floating through the air.
seasonality.summer: Full leafy canopy provides dense shade, with the downy leaf undersides creating a two-toned effect when breezes flip the foliage. Leaves remain green and full throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, creating a golden carpet beneath the tree. The timing is often earlier than many other deciduous trees.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's spreading architecture, with buds that are sticky and resinous to the touch. The furrowed bark becomes more prominent without the leafy distraction.

funFact: Swamp cottonwood is like the aquatic superhero of the poplar world - it can actually survive with its roots completely underwater for months at a time, something that would kill most other trees!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Eastern cottonwood, but swamp cottonwood has much fuzzier leaf undersides and grows in wetter spots. Memory trick: 'Swamp = soft and soggy' - both the habitat and the fuzzy leaf feel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cottonwood,' this tree is actually more closely related to aspens and is in the willow family, not related to actual cotton plants. The cotton-like seeds can be messy but are an important food source for birds and small mammals.
compareHints: Unlike quaking aspen with its flattened leaf stems that make leaves tremble, swamp cottonwood has round leaf stems and much larger, heart-shaped leaves. Eastern cottonwood has similar triangular leaves but lacks the downy undersides and prefers riverbanks over swamps. Bigtooth aspen has the large teeth on leaf edges that swamp cottonwood lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's aspens, bigtooth aspen has the largest leaf teeth - quaking aspen has tiny, fine teeth while bigtooth's are chunky and rounded.
Among New England's aspens and poplars, quaking aspen has the smallest, most finely-toothed leaves and the most constant trembling motion.
Eastern cottonwood dwarfs its poplar relatives in New England - quaking aspen and bigtooth aspen rarely exceed 50 feet, while cottonwood can reach 100+ feet.
Among New England's poplars, balsam poplar is the only one with intensely fragrant buds — quaking and bigtooth aspens have smaller, less aromatic buds.

White poplar stands apart from native New England poplars by its distinctly white, woolly leaf undersides - all our native aspens and cottonwoods have smooth, pale green to silvery undersides instead.
Among New England poplars, black poplar stands out with its distinctly dark, deeply furrowed bark - much darker than Eastern cottonwood's light gray bark or the smooth bark of aspens.
